supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters and put
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$. Let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and require
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\ne0\qquad(r\in J).$$
On the smooth product $\mathcal M_J:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times J_r\times S^2$,
use $S^2=\{(X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb R^3:X^2+Y^2+Z^2=1\}$ with its subspace
topology ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). Specify the smooth
structure by the sphere atlas of [[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]],
Definition (b): for $\varepsilon=\pm1$, delete $p_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon)$
and use $\sigma_\varepsilon(X,Y,Z)=(X,Y)/(1-\varepsilon Z)$.
For $u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $h=u_1^2+u_2^2$, its inverse is
$\sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}(u)=(2u_1,2u_2,\varepsilon(h-1))/(1+h)$;
the transition is $u\mapsto u/h$ on $h>0$. These rational maps are smooth
on their domains. The product atlas consists of
$(x^0,r,p)\mapsto(x^0,r,\sigma_\varepsilon(p))$ on
$\mathbb R\times J\times(S^2\setminus\{p_\varepsilon\})$;
its transitions leave $x^0,r$ fixed and apply the displayed sphere transition.
The product is Hausdorff and second countable by the subspace topology from
$\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^3$, whose rational balls give a countable basis.
These charts specify its maximal smooth atlas, including when $J$ is empty.
The inclusion of $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$ is smooth with injective differential
in these parametrizations; its induced unit round metric is $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]).
Orient $S^2$ by its outward unit normal: for $p\in S^2$ and
$u,v\in T_pS^2$, define
$$ (\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v):=\det(p,u,v). $$
Thus $\omega_{S^2}$ is the positive area form of $\gamma_{S^2}$, and in the
polar chart $X=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $Y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$,
$Z=\cos\theta$ it is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. The **dyonic RN
datum** is
$$g=-f(r)\,dx^0\otimes dx^0+f(r)^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2}, \qquad \mathcal F=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dx^0\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$
Here $x^0$ and $r$ have units of metres, angles on $S^2$ are dimensionless,
and $M,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres. The metric components are dimensionless
in length coordinates; the nonzero coordinate components of $\mathcal F$ have
units inherited from their coordinate Jacobians. Use the orientation
$dx^0\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$.

The set $J$ may have several connected components. On $\{f>0\}$ choose the
time orientation $\partial_{x^0}$; on $\{f<0\}$ choose $\partial_r$. These
are smooth timelike fields on their respective open subsets because
$g(\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^0})=-f<0$ when $f>0$ and
$g(\partial_r,\partial_r)=f^{-1}<0$ when $f<0$. Since $f$ has no zero on
$\mathcal M_J$, this defines a smooth time orientation on the whole product.
The sphere area form and the displayed two-form are global on $S^2$.

Let $N,S$ denote the north and south poles. On
$U_N:=S^2\setminus\{S\}$ and $U_S:=S^2\setminus\{N\}$, respectively,
local potential one-forms are
$$\mathcal A_N=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0+q_m(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad \mathcal A_S=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0-q_m(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi.$$
Each displayed potential extends smoothly over its named included pole:
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $N$ and
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $S$. Direct differentiation gives
$d\mathcal A_N=d\mathcal A_S=\mathcal F$ on the respective patches. Their
overlap difference is $2q_m\,d\phi$; it is local potential data, not a global
real gauge function on the entire sphere. The definition assumes no $U(1)$
bundle or charge quantization. To verify pole smoothness, use local coordinates
$u=X,v=Y$ near each pole. There
$d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(u^2+v^2)$. Near $N$,
$1-\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1+Z)$, so
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1+Z)$ is smooth. Near $S$,
$1+\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1-Z)$, so
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1-Z)$ is smooth. The denominators are
nonzero on the respective named patches.

null hypersurface of this form. These are local properties of the selected

$$r_\pm:=m\pm\sqrt{m^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2m}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\quad(r>0).$$
On the fixed exterior $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2$, use the exact dyonic Reissner–Nordström metric specified by the preceding mathematical definition with its mass parameter identified as $M=m$ and charges $q_e,q_m$, and set $t=x^0$. Define a real normalized spherical harmonic of degree $\ell\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ to mean a smooth real $Y:S^2\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1,\qquad \Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y,$$
where in the standard polar chart
$$\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=\frac1{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta Y)+\frac1{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\phi^2Y.$$
Here $d\omega_{S^2}$ is the area measure of the unit round metric $\gamma_{S^2}$, and $f'(r)$ denotes the ordinary derivative of $f$ with respect to $r$. Since $r_+>0$, the basepoint $r_0:=2r_+$ lies in the exterior; define the tortoise coordinate by the oriented integral $r_*(r):=\int_{r_0}^{r}f(\rho)^{-1}\,d\rho$. For any such $Y$, let $\psi(t,r,\omega)=\phi(t,r)Y(\omega)$ be a smooth real solution of $\Box_g\psi=0$, and put $U_\ell(t,r_*):=r\phi(t,r)$. Then $r_*$ is a smooth coordinate from $(r_+,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$, and
$$\partial_t^2U_\ell-\partial_{r_*}^2U_\ell+V_\ell(r_*)U_\ell=0,\qquad V_\ell(r_*):=f(r)\left(\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}+\frac{f'(r)}r\right).$$
The potential is smooth, bounded, and strictly positive on $\mathbb R$. If $U_\ell$ and its derivatives satisfy the decay assumptions of the positive matrix-potential wave-energy theorem on the time interval considered, then
$$E_\ell(t):=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R}\left((\partial_tU_\ell)^2+(\partial_{r_*}U_\ell)^2+V_\ell U_\ell^2\right)\,dr_*$$
is constant there. In the original radial coordinate, its radial derivative term is $\frac12\int_{r_+}^{\infty}f(r)|\partial_rU_\ell|^2\,dr$; this energy loses control of $\partial_rU_\ell$ as $r\downarrow r_+$. It asserts no nondegenerate horizon-crossing derivative estimate, decay estimate, or coupled Einstein–Maxwell stability result. The coordinates $t,r,r_*$ and parameters $m,q_e,q_m$ have unit metres, $f$ is dimensionless, and $V_\ell$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-2}$. If $\psi,\phi$ have a common arbitrary field unit $\Phi$, then $Y$ is dimensionless, $U_\ell$ has unit $\Phi\,\mathrm m$, and $E_\ell$ has unit $\Phi^2\,\mathrm m$.

Let $M>0$ and $Q\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $0<|Q|<M$. Put
$$r_\pm:=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2},\qquad r>r_+.$$
Use the static exterior
$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2$
with the electric specialization $q_e=Q$, $q_m=0$, and $t=x^0$ of the
Reissner--Nordström metric and potential fixed in the preceding definition.
Thus
$$g=-f\,dt^2+f^{-1}dr^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad A=-\frac Qr\,dt,\qquad A_t\longrightarrow0\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty).$$
Here $r_+$ is the positive outer root in the selected local model, not a claim
about an event horizon in a maximal spacetime. Set
$\Phi_H:=Q/r_+=A_t(\infty)-A_t(r_+)$ for this gauge.

For a complex scalar function $\psi$ in this fixed trivialization and a real
coupling $e$, put $D_a\psi:=(\partial_a-ieA_a)\psi$. Define the massless
charged wave operator in the static chart by
$$\Box_{g,A}\psi:=-f^{-1}D_t^2\psi+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r\!\left(r^2f\,\partial_r\psi\right)+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}\psi,\qquad D_t=\partial_t+\frac{ieQ}{r}.$$
The equation used here is $\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$; it is a fixed-background,
minimally coupled test-field equation and does not evolve or source $g$ or $A$.

Let $e\in\mathbb R$, $\omega>0$, and $\ell\in\mathbb N_0$. Supply a smooth
real function $Y:S^2\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1,\qquad \Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y.$$
No existence assertion about $Y$ is made. Use the tortoise coordinate
$$r_*(r):=\int_{2r_+}^{r}f(\rho)^{-1}\,d\rho,$$
which is strictly increasing because $f>0$ on the exterior. Under the
subextremal hypotheses the supplied RN scalar-coordinate result proves that
$r_*$ is a smooth coordinate from $(r_+,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$; hence
$r_*\to-\infty$ as $r\downarrow r_+$ and $r_*\to+\infty$ as $r\to\infty$.
A separated mode has the form
$$\psi(t,r,\Omega)=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)\frac{u(r_*)}{r},$$
where $A_{\mathrm{in}}\ne0$ is a fixed incident amplitude with units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m$, and the normalized complex radial function $u$ and its
reflection and transmission coefficients are dimensionless.

Write $\omega_H:=\omega-e\Phi_H=\omega-eQ/r_+$ and, for any reference length
$L>0$, define the Coulomb phase
$$\Theta(r_*):=\omega r_*-eQ\log(r/L),\qquad \Theta'(r_*):=\omega-\frac{eQf(r)}r.$$
A normalized scattering solution is a smooth radial solution of
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ for which, for some $R,T\in\mathbb C$,
$$u=e^{-i\Theta}+R e^{i\Theta}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\Theta'e^{-i\Theta}+i\Theta'R e^{i\Theta}+o(1)\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty),$$
and
$$u=T e^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\omega_HTe^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1)\quad(r\downarrow r_+).$$
The error terms tend to zero in the indicated limits. These boundary
conditions prescribe unit incoming amplitude at infinity and only the
ingoing branch at the future horizon. They define admissible scattering data;
they assert neither existence nor uniqueness of such a solution.

The logarithm in $\Theta$ is required by the long-range term
$-2\omega eQ/r$ in the asymptotic radial coefficient. Changing $L$ changes
constant phases, not flux magnitudes. A constant gauge shift changes the
frequency label, so the threshold uses the potential difference
$\Phi_H$, not an absolute value of $A_t$.

Use geometric units $G=c=1$ and length coordinates, with
$[t]=[r]=[r_*]=[M]=[Q]=[L]=\mathrm m$,
$[e]=[\omega]=\mathrm m^{-1}$, $f$ dimensionless, and $A_t$ dimensionless;
then $\Theta$ is dimensionless and each term in $\Box_{g,A}$ has units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. The coupling $e$ is the charge coupling in the
chosen field normalization; restoring SI units requires restoring the
corresponding field normalization and the charge-over-$\hbar$ coupling.
This definition excludes scalar mass, magnetic charge, mirrors, anti-de Sitter
boundaries, bound states, and complex-frequency quasinormal boundary conditions.
A scalar mass would change the propagating infinity wave number to
$\sqrt{\omega^2-\mu^2}$ and requires a different scattering normalization.
Complex-frequency quasinormal modes form a distinct non-self-adjoint spectral
problem and are not covered by the real-frequency Wronskian identity.

derivations.claim:
Put $\varpi(r)=\omega-eQ/r$. Since $A_t$ is independent of $t$,
$D_t(e^{-i\omega t}uY/r)=-i\varpi(r)e^{-i\omega t}uY/r$ and
$D_t^2(e^{-i\omega t}uY/r)=-\varpi(r)^2e^{-i\omega t}uY/r$.
The angular term is $-\ell(\ell+1)e^{-i\omega t}uY/r$. Substitution into
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ and division only by the nonzero factor
$A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}$ gives $Y(\Omega)\,B(t,r)=0$, where
$$B(t,r)=\frac{\varpi(r)^2}{f(r)}\frac{u}{r}+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r\!\left(r^2f(r)\partial_r\frac{u}{r}\right)-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^3}u.$$
Multiplying by $Y$ and integrating over $S^2$ gives $B(t,r)=0$ because
$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1$; no division by $Y$ at its zeros is used.

Since $dr_*/dr=f^{-1}$, $\partial_{r_*}=f\partial_r$, so
$r^2f\partial_r(u/r)=r\,\partial_{r_*}u-fu$. Multiplying $B=0$ by $fr$,
the radial derivative term becomes
$$\frac f r\partial_r(r\partial_{r_*}u-fu)=\frac1r\partial_{r_*}(r\partial_{r_*}u-fu)=\partial_{r_*}^2u-\frac{ff'}r u,$$
where $\partial_{r_*}r=f$ and $\partial_{r_*}f=ff'$. The other terms become
$\varpi^2u$ and $-f\ell(\ell+1)u/r^2$. Their sum is the asserted radial
equation.

Let $M>0$ and $Q\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $0<|Q|<M$. Put
$$r_\pm:=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2},\qquad r>r_+.$$
Use the static exterior
$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2$
with the electric specialization $q_e=Q$, $q_m=0$, and $t=x^0$ of the
Reissner--Nordström metric and potential fixed in the preceding definition.
Thus
$$g=-f\,dt^2+f^{-1}dr^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad A=-\frac Qr\,dt,\qquad A_t\longrightarrow0\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty).$$
Here $r_+$ is the positive outer root in the selected local model, not a claim
about an event horizon in a maximal spacetime. Set
$\Phi_H:=Q/r_+=A_t(\infty)-A_t(r_+)$ for this gauge.

For a complex scalar function $\psi$ in this fixed trivialization and a real
coupling $e$, put $D_a\psi:=(\partial_a-ieA_a)\psi$. Define the massless
charged wave operator in the static chart by
$$\Box_{g,A}\psi:=-f^{-1}D_t^2\psi+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r\!\left(r^2f\,\partial_r\psi\right)+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}\psi,\qquad D_t=\partial_t+\frac{ieQ}{r}.$$
The equation used here is $\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$; it is a fixed-background,
minimally coupled test-field equation and does not evolve or source $g$ or $A$.

Let $e\in\mathbb R$, $\omega>0$, and $\ell\in\mathbb N_0$. Supply a smooth
real function $Y:S^2\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1,\qquad \Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y.$$
No existence assertion about $Y$ is made. Use the tortoise coordinate
$$r_*(r):=\int_{2r_+}^{r}f(\rho)^{-1}\,d\rho,$$
which is strictly increasing because $f>0$ on the exterior. Under the
subextremal hypotheses the supplied RN scalar-coordinate result proves that
$r_*$ is a smooth coordinate from $(r_+,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$; hence
$r_*\to-\infty$ as $r\downarrow r_+$ and $r_*\to+\infty$ as $r\to\infty$.
A separated mode has the form
$$\psi(t,r,\Omega)=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)\frac{u(r_*)}{r},$$
where $A_{\mathrm{in}}\ne0$ is a fixed incident amplitude with units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m$, and the normalized complex radial function $u$ and its
reflection and transmission coefficients are dimensionless.

Write $\omega_H:=\omega-e\Phi_H=\omega-eQ/r_+$ and, for any reference length
$L>0$, define the Coulomb phase
$$\Theta(r_*):=\omega r_*-eQ\log(r/L),\qquad \Theta'(r_*):=\omega-\frac{eQf(r)}r.$$
A normalized scattering solution is a smooth radial solution of
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ for which, for some $R,T\in\mathbb C$,
$$u=e^{-i\Theta}+R e^{i\Theta}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\Theta'e^{-i\Theta}+i\Theta'R e^{i\Theta}+o(1)\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty),$$
and
$$u=T e^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\omega_HTe^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1)\quad(r\downarrow r_+).$$
The error terms tend to zero in the indicated limits. These boundary
conditions prescribe unit incoming amplitude at infinity and only the
ingoing branch at the future horizon. They define admissible scattering data;
they assert neither existence nor uniqueness of such a solution.

The logarithm in $\Theta$ is required by the long-range term
$-2\omega eQ/r$ in the asymptotic radial coefficient. Changing $L$ changes
constant phases, not flux magnitudes. A constant gauge shift changes the
frequency label, so the threshold uses the potential difference
$\Phi_H$, not an absolute value of $A_t$.

Use geometric units $G=c=1$ and length coordinates, with
$[t]=[r]=[r_*]=[M]=[Q]=[L]=\mathrm m$,
$[e]=[\omega]=\mathrm m^{-1}$, $f$ dimensionless, and $A_t$ dimensionless;
then $\Theta$ is dimensionless and each term in $\Box_{g,A}$ has units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. The coupling $e$ is the charge coupling in the
chosen field normalization; restoring SI units requires restoring the
corresponding field normalization and the charge-over-$\hbar$ coupling.
This definition excludes scalar mass, magnetic charge, mirrors, anti-de Sitter
boundaries, bound states, and complex-frequency quasinormal boundary conditions.
A scalar mass would change the propagating infinity wave number to
$\sqrt{\omega^2-\mu^2}$ and requires a different scattering normalization.
Complex-frequency quasinormal modes form a distinct non-self-adjoint spectral
problem and are not covered by the real-frequency Wronskian identity.

derivations.claim:
Differentiate $j=\operatorname{Im}(\overline u\,u')$. The radial equation
gives
$$j'=\operatorname{Im}(\overline{u'}u'+\overline u\,u'')=\operatorname{Im}(|u'|^2-K|u|^2)=0,$$
because both terms inside the last imaginary part are real by [F2]. Thus
$j$ is constant along the exterior.

At infinity, $\Theta'=\omega-eQf/r\to\omega$. Substitution of the
Definition's differentiated asymptotics into $j$ gives
$j_\infty=\omega(|R|^2-1)$: the incident and reflected diagonal terms are
$-\omega$ and $\omega|R|^2$, while the two cross terms have real sum. At the
horizon the asymptotics give $j_H=-\omega_H|T|^2$. Equating these limits by
step 1.1 and dividing by $\omega>0$ proves the identity. If
$0<\omega<eQ/r_+$ then $\omega_H<0$; when $T\ne0$ the identity yields
$|R|^2=1+(-\omega_H/\omega)|T|^2>1$. The unit incoming and reflected
asymptotic flux magnitudes are $\omega$ and $\omega|R|^2$, so the stated
radial-flux comparison follows.

Let the metric, gauge, parameters, tortoise coordinate, harmonic $Y$, and
operator be exactly those of the charged radial scattering definition. For
$\varpi(r):=\omega-eQ/r$, a smooth separated solution
$\psi=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)u(r_*)/r$ of
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ has radial function satisfying
$$\frac{d^2u}{dr_*^2}+\left[\left(\omega-\frac{eQ}{r}\right)^2-f(r)\left(\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}+\frac{f'(r)}r\right)\right]u=0.$$
Here $f'$ denotes the derivative with respect to $r$, and derivatives of $u$
are with respect to $r_*$.

Let $u$ be any scattering solution as defined on the fixed subextremal electric
RN exterior, with real $\omega>0$, real $e,Q$, unit incoming amplitude, and
reflection and transmission coefficients $R,T$. Then its radial Wronskian
flux $j:=\operatorname{Im}(\overline u\,\partial_{r_*}u)$ is constant and
$$|R|^2=1-\frac{\omega-eQ/r_+}{\omega}|T|^2.$$
Consequently, if $0<\omega<eQ/r_+$ and $T\ne0$, the reflected radial flux
magnitude exceeds the incident radial flux magnitude, since their ratio is
$|R|^2>1$. This is conditional on an admitted scattering solution and does not
assert its existence, a complex-frequency mode, or a nonlinear instability.

Let $M>0$ and $Q\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $0<|Q|<M$. Put
$$r_\pm:=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2},\qquad r>r_+.$$
Use the static exterior
$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2$
with the electric specialization $q_e=Q$, $q_m=0$, and $t=x^0$ of the
Reissner--Nordström metric and potential fixed in the preceding definition.
Thus
$$g=-f\,dt^2+f^{-1}dr^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad A=-\frac Qr\,dt,\qquad A_t\longrightarrow0\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty).$$
Here $r_+$ is the positive outer root in the selected local model, not a claim
about an event horizon in a maximal spacetime. Set
$\Phi_H:=Q/r_+=A_t(\infty)-A_t(r_+)$ for this gauge.

For a complex scalar function $\psi$ in this fixed trivialization and a real
coupling $e$, put $D_a\psi:=(\partial_a-ieA_a)\psi$. Define the massless
charged wave operator in the static chart by
$$\Box_{g,A}\psi:=-f^{-1}D_t^2\psi+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r\!\left(r^2f\,\partial_r\psi\right)+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}\psi,\qquad D_t=\partial_t+\frac{ieQ}{r}.$$
The equation used here is $\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$; it is a fixed-background,
minimally coupled test-field equation and does not evolve or source $g$ or $A$.

Let $e\in\mathbb R$, $\omega>0$, and $\ell\in\mathbb N_0$. Supply a smooth
real function $Y:S^2\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1,\qquad \Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y.$$
No existence assertion about $Y$ is made. Use the tortoise coordinate
$$r_*(r):=\int_{2r_+}^{r}f(\rho)^{-1}\,d\rho,$$
which is strictly increasing because $f>0$ on the exterior. Under the
subextremal hypotheses the supplied RN scalar-coordinate result proves that
$r_*$ is a smooth coordinate from $(r_+,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$; hence
$r_*\to-\infty$ as $r\downarrow r_+$ and $r_*\to+\infty$ as $r\to\infty$.
A separated mode has the form
$$\psi(t,r,\Omega)=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)\frac{u(r_*)}{r},$$
where $A_{\mathrm{in}}\ne0$ is a fixed incident amplitude with units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m$, and the normalized complex radial function $u$ and its
reflection and transmission coefficients are dimensionless.

Write $\omega_H:=\omega-e\Phi_H=\omega-eQ/r_+$ and, for any reference length
$L>0$, define the Coulomb phase
$$\Theta(r_*):=\omega r_*-eQ\log(r/L),\qquad \Theta'(r_*):=\omega-\frac{eQf(r)}r.$$
A normalized scattering solution is a smooth radial solution of
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ for which, for some $R,T\in\mathbb C$,
$$u=e^{-i\Theta}+R e^{i\Theta}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\Theta'e^{-i\Theta}+i\Theta'R e^{i\Theta}+o(1)\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty),$$
and
$$u=T e^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\omega_HTe^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1)\quad(r\downarrow r_+).$$
The error terms tend to zero in the indicated limits. These boundary
conditions prescribe unit incoming amplitude at infinity and only the
ingoing branch at the future horizon. They define admissible scattering data;
they assert neither existence nor uniqueness of such a solution.

The logarithm in $\Theta$ is required by the long-range term
$-2\omega eQ/r$ in the asymptotic radial coefficient. Changing $L$ changes
constant phases, not flux magnitudes. A constant gauge shift changes the
frequency label, so the threshold uses the potential difference
$\Phi_H$, not an absolute value of $A_t$.

Use geometric units $G=c=1$ and length coordinates, with
$[t]=[r]=[r_*]=[M]=[Q]=[L]=\mathrm m$,
$[e]=[\omega]=\mathrm m^{-1}$, $f$ dimensionless, and $A_t$ dimensionless;
then $\Theta$ is dimensionless and each term in $\Box_{g,A}$ has units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. The coupling $e$ is the charge coupling in the
chosen field normalization; restoring SI units requires restoring the
corresponding field normalization and the charge-over-$\hbar$ coupling.
This definition excludes scalar mass, magnetic charge, mirrors, anti-de Sitter
boundaries, bound states, and complex-frequency quasinormal boundary conditions.
A scalar mass would change the propagating infinity wave number to
$\sqrt{\omega^2-\mu^2}$ and requires a different scattering normalization.
Complex-frequency quasinormal modes form a distinct non-self-adjoint spectral
problem and are not covered by the real-frequency Wronskian identity.

derivations.claim:
Write $x=r_*$ and use the choices in [A1]--[A2]. By [F3], $x$ ranges over
all of $\mathbb R$ and $dr/dx=f$. The charged radial
equation [F1] becomes
$$u''(x)+\bigl(\omega^2-V(x)\bigr)u(x)=0,\qquad
V(x):=\frac{f(r(x))f'(r(x))}{r(x)}.$$
The definition gives $dr/dx=f$ and $f(r)=(r-r_+)(r-r_-)/r^2$. Since
$r_+>M>r_-$ and $r_+r_-=Q^2$, we have $f(r)>0$ and $Mr>Mr_+>Q^2$
for $r>r_+$, so $f'(r)=2(Mr-Q^2)/r^3>0$ and $V>0$. Thus $V$ is smooth
and real. Moreover,
$$\int_{\mathbb R}|V(x)|\,dx=\int_{r_+}^{\infty}\frac{f'(r)}r\,dr
=\int_{r_+}^{\infty}\frac{2(Mr-Q^2)}{r^4}\,dr<\infty.$$

Define $u_-$ by the Volterra equation
$$u_-(x)=e^{-i\omega x}+\frac1\omega\int_{-\infty}^{x}
\sin\!\bigl(\omega(x-y)\bigr)V(y)u_-(y)\,dy.$$
Iteration gives a uniformly convergent Neumann series: the absolute value of
its $n$th iterated term is at most
$\|V\|_{L^1(\mathbb R)}^n/(\omega^n n!)$, using $|\sin z|\le1$ for real $z$
and the ordered integration region. The sum is bounded on $\mathbb R$; differentiating
the integral equation shows it is a smooth solution of the equation in
step 1.1. The tail integrals tend to zero as $x\to-\infty$, and differentiation
under the integral gives
$$u_-(x)=e^{-i\omega x}+o(1),\qquad
u_-'(x)=-i\omega e^{-i\omega x}+o(1)\quad(x\to-\infty).$$

Since $V u_-\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, expanding the sine in step 2.1 into
exponentials and replacing the upper integration limit by $+\infty$ gives
$$u_-(x)=a e^{-i\omega x}+b e^{i\omega x}+o(1),\qquad
u_-'(x)=-i\omega a e^{-i\omega x}+i\omega b e^{i\omega x}+o(1)$$
as $x\to+\infty$, where
$$a=1-\frac1{2i\omega}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{i\omega y}V(y)u_-(y)\,dy,
\qquad b=\frac1{2i\omega}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-i\omega y}V(y)u_-(y)\,dy.$$
The same tail estimate after differentiating the integral equation proves the
displayed derivative asymptotic.

For $j=\operatorname{Im}(\overline{u_-}u_-')$, the real-coefficient
equation in step 1.1 gives $j'=0$. The horizon asymptotics in step 2.1 yield
$j=-\omega$, while step 3.1 yields $j=\omega(|b|^2-|a|^2)$ at infinity;
the two oscillatory cross terms have real sum and contribute no imaginary part.
Hence $|a|^2=|b|^2+1$, so $a\ne0$. Put $u=u_-/a$, $R=b/a$, and $T=1/a$.
Then $u$ has the asymptotics in [F3], with unit incoming amplitude and only
the ingoing branch at the horizon. The separated-wave substitution in the
proof of [F1] is reversible here: $Y$ is a nonzero constant, $A_{\mathrm{in}}$
and $fr$ are nonzero, and each displayed step is an equality. Therefore
$\psi=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y u/r$ solves $\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ and is
an admitted scattering solution for any fixed nonzero allowed
$A_{\mathrm{in}}$.

Apply [F2] to this constructed solution. Since $e=0$ and $T=1/a\ne0$,
$$|R|^2=1-|T|^2=1-|a|^{-2}<1.$$
Thus this nonzero-charge background admits a neutral mode whose reflected
radial flux is less than the incident flux, contradicting the universal
amplification statement.
